\begin{document}

\title{Feedback-Corrected Conformal Prediction for\\ Spatiotemporal Crime Forecasting}

\author{Himanshu~Bairwa%
\thanks{H. Bairwa is with the Department of Computer Science. Corresponding author e-mail: bairwahimanshu29@gmail.com.}%
}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Crime records are not crime. Records are produced by a loop: records direct
patrols, patrols determine where crime is looked for, and the loop amplifies
whatever disparity it began with. A forecaster fit on such records can be
exactly calibrated against the record and badly wrong about reality, and no
validation on records distinguishes the two cases. We formalize the loop as a
fixed point, derive the elasticity with which it amplifies latent disparity, and
invert it. The inversion is exact: deflating the recorded rate by the fitted
recording multiplier recovers the latent rate identically, and the intervals are
valid conditional on a retention rule we state and measure. In simulation at
feedback gain $0.85$, intervals calibrated on the record cover latent incidence
$16.2\%$ of the time against a $90\%$ target; the corrected intervals hold
$93.0\%$, on the $15\%$ of cells they do not abstain on. Under bounded
misspecification a $\Gamma$-inflated interval retains nominal coverage at a
tabulated width cost.
The forecaster is a dual-graph GATv2 model with a zero-inflated negative binomial
head and a five-seed ensemble: CRPS $2.8267$ (Chicago) and $3.1401$ (New York) on
2023, ahead of four deep baselines in all eight Diebold--Mariano comparisons at
$p < 2\times10^{-6}$, with $90.75\%$ and $90.02\%$ conformal coverage under a
pre-registered $3\%$ disparity ceiling. Three limits: a rolling historical average
beats every deep baseline we ran; Chicago's probability integral transform is
non-uniform at $p = 5.25\times10^{-47}$; and the feedback gain is not
point-identified, so real-data results are sensitivity analyses.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
Conformal prediction, crime forecasting, algorithmic fairness, feedback loops,
measurement error, zero-inflated models, graph neural networks.
\end{IEEEkeywords}

% =====================================================================
\section{Introduction}
% =====================================================================
\IEEEPARstart{A}{crime} forecast is also an instrument for producing the data that
will train its successor. Weather forecasts do not change the weather. Crime
forecasts direct patrols, patrols determine where crime is looked for, and crime
that nobody looks for goes unrecorded. Send officers to a block and its recorded
rate rises even if the underlying rate holds perfectly still. The training data is
an artifact of past decisions by the system one is trying to improve.

The consequence is a blind spot in validation, and it is structural rather than a
matter of insufficient care. Hold out a year, compute the Continuous Ranked
Probability Score (CRPS), check interval coverage: passing every such test
establishes that the model predicts \emph{records} well and settles nothing about
whether it predicts \emph{crime} well. The two quantities diverge precisely where
the stakes are highest, in the neighbourhoods that were over-policed to begin
with. Ensign \emph{et al.}~\cite{ensign2018runaway} named the loop and showed it
runs away. van Amsterdam \emph{et al.}~\cite{vanamsterdam2025when} characterized
the general pattern: a model accurate and harmful at once, undetectable by passive
validation. Neither supplies a correction.

This paper supplies one, and states the conditions under which it holds.

Let latent incidence $\lambda_s$ in area $s$ be unobserved. A policy allocates
attention $a_s = \varphi(\mu_s)$ from the recorded-rate estimate $\mu_s$;
recording is attention-dependent, $y_s \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_s\, g(a_s))$
with $g$ increasing; and a learner that fits the records converges to the
self-consistent equilibrium
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:fixedpoint}
\mu_s = \lambda_s\, g\!\left(\varphi(\mu_s)\right).
\end{equation}
Section~\ref{sec:theory} develops three consequences of \eqref{eq:fixedpoint}: a
feedback gain $\kappa$ that is the product of two log-elasticities, an
amplification law with a pole at $\kappa = 1$, and an exact inversion of the
recording map. On credit, we are deliberately narrow. The amplification form
$1/(1-\kappa)$ is classical --- the closed-loop gain of a feedback amplifier, and
in economics the social multiplier of Glaeser, Sacerdote and
Scheinkman~\cite{glaeser2003social} --- and we claim neither. The contribution is
the constructive step: deflate the record by the fitted recording multiplier and
issue intervals valid for $\lambda$ rather than for $y$, abstaining where the
correction ceases to be trustworthy.

The empirical picture is as follows. CIVIC-SAFE predicts a full Zero-Inflated
Negative Binomial (ZINB) distribution per area--week--category and attains CRPS
2.8267 (Chicago) and 3.1401 (NYC) on 2023, ahead of every baseline we ran, with
all eight head-to-head Diebold--Mariano comparisons against deep baselines
significant at $p < 2\times10^{-6}$. Fig.~\ref{fig:architecture} illustrates the
end-to-end architecture across all six pipeline stages. Post-hoc conformal
calibration attains 90.75\% and 90.02\% coverage against a 90\% target while
holding demographic coverage disparity at 0.0238 and 0.0286, both under a ceiling
fixed at 0.03 in advance. The correction then does what record-level calibration
cannot: at $\kappa = 0.85$ in a closed-loop simulation, intervals calibrated on the
record cover the latent process 16.2\% of the time while corrected intervals hold
93.0\%. On real Chicago and NYC records the correction reduces
recorded-exposure disparity for the higher-minority stratum by 58\% and 61\%.

Four results cut against us, and we state them here rather than in a footnote.
A rolling historical average beats every deep spatiotemporal baseline in our
comparison set, in both cities, so the eight Diebold--Mariano wins are wins over
models a moving average also beats; CIVIC-SAFE is the only method in the study
that improves on the trailing mean, and by 3.6\% and 4.9\%. Chicago's PIT
histogram is not uniform ($\chi^2 = 241.84$ on nine degrees of freedom,
$p = 5.25 \times 10^{-47}$), so the ZINB is misspecified in Chicago's right tail,
and the spatial residuals concur with 65 of 77 areas low. A single seed loses to
TFT-ZINB, so the win rests on ensembling. And the corrected intervals at
$\kappa = 0.85$ abstain on 85\% of cells, so the headline $16\% \to 93\%$ compares
two different denominators --- a fact Theorem~\ref{thm:deflation}(iv) formalizes
rather than excuses. Section~\ref{sec:limitations} collects these.

\begin{figure*}[!t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.98\textwidth]{fig_architecture.pdf}
  \caption{End-to-end system architecture of CIVIC-SAFE across six pipeline stages.
  \textbf{Stage 1 (Inputs \& Urban Graphs):} Weekly count tensors $\mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{N}^{S \times T \times C}$ alongside dual spatial adjacencies ($\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{queen}}$ for geographic contiguity and $\mathcal{E}_{k\mathrm{NN}}$ for demographic similarity) and exogenous census covariates.
  \textbf{Stage 2 (Sequential V1 Backbone):} Dual-graph GATv2 spatial attention coupled with staged temporal attention and a three-parameter Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial (ZINB) output head $(\pi, \mu, r)$ with dispersion regularization.
  \textbf{Stage 3 (Ensemble):} Five-seed EMOS ensemble trained with entropy-regularized CRPS minimization to distill robust epistemic representations.
  \textbf{Stage 4 (Conformal Calibration):} Finite-sample distribution-free CQR interval calibration across ten conformal variants evaluated under a pre-registered 3\% demographic disparity ceiling.
  \textbf{Stage 5 (Latent Deflation Operator):} Exact fixed-point inversion $\hat{\lambda}_s = \mu_s / (\mu_s/M)^\kappa$ paired with a bounded abstention guard that withholds predictions when multiplier $m_s \notin [\bar{m}^{-1}, \bar{m}]$, restoring valid latent coverage from $16.2\%$ to $93.0\%$.
  \textbf{Stage 6 (Downstream Policy):} Over-allocation constrained coverage (OICC) and equitable dispatch achieving $98.9\%$ target hits with a $76\%$ reduction in exposure disparity.}
  \label{fig:architecture}
\end{figure*}

\subsection{Contributions}
\begin{enumerate}
  \item A feedback-corrected conformal predictor that restores coverage of the
  latent process from a biased record, with principled abstention
  (Section~\ref{sec:latent}). Prior work diagnoses this pathology; to our
  knowledge this is the first construction that corrects it.
  \item A coordinate-free form of the amplification elasticity, with $\kappa$ a
  product of two log-elasticities, and the disparity power law that follows
  (Theorem~\ref{thm:amplification}) --- a sharpening
  of~\cite{ensign2018runaway} that credits~\cite{glaeser2003social} for the gain.
  \item An exactness result for the deflation (Theorem~\ref{thm:deflation}),
  together with the sensitivity bound that motivates the abstention rule and the
  conditional nature of the resulting guarantee.
  \item A competitive applied forecaster with honest calibration: ten conformal
  variants compared under constraint-based selection against a pre-registered
  fairness ceiling, plus a full accounting of failure modes.
\end{enumerate}

% =====================================================================
\section{Related Work}
% =====================================================================
\textbf{Spatiotemporal count forecasting.} ZINB output heads on graph networks
are established for sparse urban counts. STZINB-GNN~\cite{zhuang2022uncertainty}
pairs a zero-inflated negative binomial likelihood with a spatiotemporal graph
encoder, and STMGNN-ZINB~\cite{wang2024spatiotemporal} adds multi-graph fusion.
Our predictor sits in this family and we make no architectural novelty claim for
it. GATv2~\cite{brody2022attentive} supplies the attention operator; we use two
adjacency structures rather than one.

\textbf{Conformal prediction.} Split conformal prediction gives
distribution-free finite-sample coverage under exchangeability. Conformalized
quantile regression~\cite{romano2019conformalized} supplies our score, adaptive
conformal inference~\cite{gibbs2021adaptive} handles drift by updating the
miscoverage target online, and equalized conditional risk
control~\cite{feldman2021improving} gives per-group coverage through
concentration bounds. All are applied here as published. What conformal
prediction guarantees, though, is coverage of the variable you calibrated
against --- the record. That is the gap this paper addresses.

The nearest-looking remedy is weighted conformal prediction under covariate
shift~\cite{tibshirani2019conformal}, and it is worth saying precisely why it does
not close that gap. Weighted CP reweights the calibration scores by a covariate
likelihood ratio $w(x) = dQ_X/dP_X(x)$, and its validity rests on the conditional
outcome law being invariant, $P(Y \mid X) = Q(Y \mid X)$: the covariate marginal
is allowed to move, the outcome mechanism is not. Our distortion is the opposite
kind. The covariates do not shift. The \emph{outcome} does, because attention
multiplies the recording intensity, so $P(Y \mid X)$ is exactly what the feedback
loop bends --- and the quantity we want to cover, $\lambda$, is never observed in
any sample. There is no pair of covariate distributions here and therefore no
density ratio to estimate; the object that needs inverting is the multiplicative
recording factor $m_s$ of \eqref{eq:deflation}.

Stated more generally, the covariate-shift line of work extends \emph{which}
exchangeability condition a calibration set must satisfy --- from plain
exchangeability, to weighted exchangeability under covariate shift, to online
adaptation under drift --- while holding the target variable fixed. We move along
a different axis: the target variable itself changes, from the recorded $y$ to the
latent $\lambda$. The two are composable rather than competing, since weighted CP
could be applied to the deflated rate if the covariates shifted as well.
Section~\ref{sec:calibration} makes the structural version of this argument, which
turns out to cover the whole reweighting family and not just the covariate-shift
member of it.

\textbf{Feedback loops in predictive policing.} Ensign
\emph{et al.}~\cite{ensign2018runaway} formalized the runaway loop with
attention-dependent recording and showed a P\'olya-urn model drives allocation to
a degenerate fixed point. We differ in two ways: our amplification is a smooth
power law with a finite pole at $\kappa = 1$ rather than unconditional runaway,
and we supply a correction. Hashimoto
\emph{et al.}~\cite{hashimoto2018fairness} and Wyllie
\emph{et al.}~\cite{wyllie2024fairness} study disparity amplification in
retraining loops empirically, without a closed-form exponent or a fix.

\textbf{Performativity and identification.} That predictions change the world
they predict is the subject of performative
prediction~\cite{perdomo2020performative}, and Perdomo~\cite{perdomo2025revisiting}
shows a predictor can pass every observable calibration check while being
performatively useless. The distinction we need is sharper: here a latent target
$\lambda$ is genuinely different from the recorded $y$, so the failure is a
coverage failure against an unobserved variable. Performative risk
control~\cite{li2025performative} controls risk on \emph{observed} outcomes,
which is the opposite of what is needed. That the pathology is undetectable
passively but identifiable under perturbation is a known
template~\cite{mendler2022anticipating}; we use its difference-in-differences
instantiation rather than claiming the principle.

\textbf{Detection-shock natural experiments.} Staggered acoustic gunshot
detection rollouts have been used as quasi-experiments for recorded crime
outcomes~\cite{connealy2024staggered}. Those studies estimate reduced-form
treatment effects. We reinterpret the same design as a way to estimate a
structural recording elasticity, which is the methodological move we do claim.

% =====================================================================
\section{Feedback Amplification and Latent Recovery}
\label{sec:theory}
% =====================================================================
This section states what follows from \eqref{eq:fixedpoint}. Throughout,
$M = \frac{1}{S}\sum_{s} \mu_s$ denotes the mean recorded rate, and all
elasticities are evaluated at an interior fixed point.

\begin{definition}[Closed-loop feedback gain]
\label{def:kappa}
The feedback gain of the recording loop is the product of the allocation
elasticity and the detection elasticity,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:kappa}
\kappa \;=\; \left(\frac{d \log a}{d \log \mu}\right)
             \left(\frac{d \log g}{d \log a}\right),
\end{equation}
that is, how strongly allocation responds to the record times how strongly
recording responds to allocation.
\end{definition}

Writing $\varphi(\mu) = (\mu/M)^{\beta}$ for the allocation policy and
$g(a) = a^{\rho}$ for the recording response makes both elasticities in
\eqref{eq:kappa} constant, with $\beta$ the \emph{policy elasticity} (how
aggressively allocation chases the record) and $\rho$ the \emph{detection
elasticity} (how much extra attention converts into extra recorded incidents).
Then $\kappa = \beta\rho$, and this is the parameterization we simulate.
Fig.~\ref{fig:feedback_loop} contrasts the resulting runaway feedback dynamics
against CIVIC-SAFE's deflation and abstention recovery mechanism.
Table~\ref{tab:notation} collects the symbols used throughout.

\begin{theorem}[Feedback amplification]
\label{thm:amplification}
Let $\varphi$ and $g$ be smooth and increasing, and let $\mu$ be an interior fixed
point of \eqref{eq:fixedpoint} at which $\kappa < 1$.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item[(i)] \emph{(Local elasticity.)} The recorded rate responds to the latent
  rate with elasticity
  \begin{equation}
  \label{eq:elasticity}
  \frac{d \log \mu_s}{d \log \lambda_s} \;=\; \frac{1}{1 - \kappa}.
  \end{equation}
  \item[(ii)] \emph{(Global power law.)} If in addition $\kappa$ does not vary
  with $\mu$ --- as under $\varphi(\mu) = (\mu/M)^{\beta}$ and $g(a) = a^{\rho}$,
  which give $\kappa = \beta\rho$ --- then $\mu \propto \lambda^{1/(1-\kappa)}$,
  so for two groups with true incidence ratio
  $\Delta_{\lambda} = \lambda_1 / \lambda_2$ the recorded ratio is
  \begin{equation}
  \label{eq:powerlaw}
  \Delta_y \;=\; \left(\Delta_{\lambda}\right)^{1/(1-\kappa)},
  \end{equation}
  a power law with a pole at $\kappa^{*} = 1$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{IEEEproof}
(i) Take logarithms of \eqref{eq:fixedpoint}:
$\log \mu_s = \log \lambda_s + \log g(\varphi(\mu_s))$. Write
$E = d \log \mu_s / d \log \lambda_s$ for the elasticity of interest.
Differentiating with respect to $\log \lambda_s$ and applying the chain rule to
the second term gives
\begin{equation}
E = 1 + \left(\frac{d \log g}{d \log a}\right)
        \left(\frac{d \log a}{d \log \mu}\right) E
  = 1 + \kappa E,
\end{equation}
where the bracketed product is $\kappa$ by Definition~\ref{def:kappa}. Since
$\kappa < 1$, solving gives $(1-\kappa)E = 1$, which is \eqref{eq:elasticity}.

(ii) Under the constant-elasticity parameterization the conclusion follows by
algebra rather than by integrating \eqref{eq:elasticity}, which is worth doing
because it exhibits the proportionality constant explicitly. The fixed point
$\mu_s = \lambda_s(\mu_s/M)^{\kappa}$ in logarithms is
$\log\mu_s = \log\lambda_s + \kappa(\log\mu_s - \log M)$, so
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:closedform}
\log \mu_s = \frac{\log \lambda_s - \kappa \log M}{1 - \kappa},
\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad
\mu_s = \lambda_s^{1/(1-\kappa)}\, M^{-\kappa/(1-\kappa)}.
\end{equation}
The factor $M^{-\kappa/(1-\kappa)}$ is a single scalar shared by every cell,
because $M$ is one mean for the whole panel. It therefore cancels on taking the
ratio of two groups, and \eqref{eq:powerlaw} follows with no residual constant.
\end{IEEEproof}

Three remarks. The exponent is finite for every $\kappa < 1$, so amplification is
smooth rather than the winner-take-all collapse of~\cite{ensign2018runaway}.

Part (i) holds for any smooth increasing $\varphi, g$ and depends on them only
through the product $\kappa$, which is the sense in which the elasticity is
coordinate-free. Part (ii) is the stronger statement and genuinely needs
$\kappa$ constant: for general $\varphi, g$ the gain varies with $\mu$, and hence
with $\lambda$, so no single global exponent exists. We therefore treat $\kappa$
as a \emph{local} elasticity at the fixed point rather than a universal
constant, and read \eqref{eq:powerlaw} as the constant-gain idealization that our
simulations instantiate.

That the constant in \eqref{eq:closedform} is common across cells is not a
convenience of the algebra; it is the same fact that makes
Theorem~\ref{thm:deflation}(i) exact. Both statements are rearrangements of one
identity, read in opposite directions --- forward from $\lambda$ to $\mu$ here,
backward from $\mu$ to $\lambda$ there.

Read backwards, \eqref{eq:powerlaw} answers the question a policymaker actually
asks, which is not how much a loop amplifies but how much of an observed gap is
real.

\begin{corollary}[Disparity attribution]
\label{cor:attribution}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:amplification}(ii), a recorded
between-group ratio $\Delta_y$ corresponds to a true ratio
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:attribution}
\Delta_{\lambda} = \Delta_y^{\,1-\kappa},
\end{equation}
so the fraction of a recorded log-disparity attributable to feedback rather than
to incidence is exactly $\kappa$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{IEEEproof}
Invert \eqref{eq:powerlaw}, which is a bijection on $(0,\infty)$ for
$\kappa < 1$. Taking logarithms,
$\log\Delta_y - \log\Delta_{\lambda} = \kappa \log\Delta_y$.
\end{IEEEproof}

The arithmetic is worth spelling out because it is easy to underrate. At
$\kappa = 0.5$ a recorded $2{:}1$ gap is a true $1.41{:}1$ gap; at
$\kappa = 0.6$ a recorded $3{:}1$ gap is a true $1.55{:}1$ gap; at
$\kappa = 0.85$ a recorded $5{:}1$ gap is a true $1.27{:}1$ gap. Verified against
the numerical fixed point to $10^{-12}$ relative error across
$\kappa \in \{0.3, 0.5, 0.6, 0.85\}$. Two consequences follow, in opposite
directions, and honesty requires both. A recorded disparity is a poor estimate of
a real one, and reporting recorded gaps as though they measured incidence
overstates them by a factor that grows without bound as $\kappa \to 1$. But
\eqref{eq:attribution} is not license to dismiss recorded disparity as an
artifact: $\Delta_{\lambda} > 1$ whenever $\Delta_y > 1$, so the loop amplifies a
real gap rather than manufacturing one from nothing. What it manufactures is the
\emph{magnitude}.

Stability is immediate in logarithms. Under the power-law parameterization the
fixed-point iteration is
$\log\mu \leftarrow \log\lambda + \kappa(\log\mu - \log M)$ with $M$ the current
mean, so in log coordinates its Jacobian is
$\kappa\left(I - \mathbf{1}w^{\!\top}\right)$ with
$w_j = \mu_j / (S M)$ summing to one. That matrix is $\kappa$ times a rank-one
perturbation of the identity whose eigenvalues are $1$ with multiplicity $S-1$
and $0$, so the spectral radius is exactly $\kappa$ and the iteration contracts
precisely when $\kappa < 1$ --- the same threshold that produces the pole in
\eqref{eq:powerlaw}.

\subsection{Deflation recovers the latent rate exactly}
Under the constant-elasticity parameterization, \eqref{eq:fixedpoint} becomes
$\mu_s = \lambda_s (\mu_s/M)^{\kappa}$. Define the \emph{recording multiplier}
and the deflated rate
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:deflation}
m_s = \left(\frac{\mu_s}{M}\right)^{\kappa},
\qquad
\hat{\lambda}_s = \frac{\mu_s}{m_s} = M^{\kappa}\,\mu_s^{1-\kappa}.
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Exact latent recovery and conditional coverage]
\label{thm:deflation}
Let $\mu$ satisfy $\mu_s = \lambda_s(\mu_s/M)^{\kappa}$ with $\kappa < 1$ and
$M$ the mean of the same $\mu$. Then
\begin{enumerate}
  \item[(i)] \emph{(Exactness.)} $\hat{\lambda}_s = \lambda_s$ for every $s$ ---
  the deflation \eqref{eq:deflation} is the exact algebraic inverse of the
  recording fixed point, with no unidentified constant.
  \item[(ii)] \emph{(Coverage.)} Consequently, if $y^{\mathrm{lat}}_s \sim
  \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_s)$ and $\kappa$ is known, then writing $Q^{\mathrm{Pois}}_p(\cdot)$
  for the Poisson quantile function, the interval at the deflated rate,
  \begin{equation}
  \label{eq:latent_interval}
  \widehat{C}_s = \left[\,
    Q^{\mathrm{Pois}}_{\alpha/2}(\hat{\lambda}_s),\;
    Q^{\mathrm{Pois}}_{1-\alpha/2}(\hat{\lambda}_s)
  \,\right],
  \end{equation}
  covers $y^{\mathrm{lat}}_s$ with probability at least $1-\alpha$, the
  inequality being due only to lattice discreteness.
  \item[(iii)] \emph{(Sensitivity.)} Under an estimate $\hat\kappa \ne \kappa$,
  \begin{equation}
  \label{eq:sensitivity}
  \log \hat{\lambda}_s - \log \lambda_s
   = (\kappa - \hat\kappa)\,\log\!\left(\mu_s / M\right),
  \end{equation}
  so on the retained set
  $\mathcal{R} = \{s : \hat\kappa < \kappa_{\mathrm{run}},\;
   m_s \in [\bar{m}^{-1}, \bar{m}]\}$ the log-error is bounded by
  $|\kappa - \hat\kappa|\,(\log \bar{m})/\hat\kappa$.
  \item[(iv)] \emph{(Conditionality.)} $\mathcal{R}$ is determined by $\mu$ alone
  and by no outcome, so applying the same rule to calibration and test cells
  leaves the guarantee valid \emph{conditional on retention}. It says nothing
  about the cells where the system abstains.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{IEEEproof}
(i) The fixed point rearranges directly to
$\lambda_s = \mu_s (\mu_s/M)^{-\kappa}$, which is the definition of
$\hat\lambda_s$ in \eqref{eq:deflation}; the two expressions are identical, so
$\hat\lambda_s = \lambda_s$. Note this uses the \emph{same} normalization $M$ on
both sides, which is what removes the constant that a
$\mu \propto \lambda^{1/(1-\kappa)}$ argument would otherwise leave free.
(ii) is immediate from (i): $\widehat{C}_s$ in \eqref{eq:latent_interval} is
built at the true rate, and Poisson quantile intervals are conservative on a
lattice.
(iii) From \eqref{eq:deflation},
$\log\hat\lambda_s = \log\mu_s - \hat\kappa \log(\mu_s/M)$, while (i) gives
$\log\lambda_s = \log\mu_s - \kappa\log(\mu_s/M)$; subtracting yields
\eqref{eq:sensitivity}. On $\mathcal{R}$, $m_s \in [\bar{m}^{-1},\bar{m}]$ means
$|\hat\kappa \log(\mu_s/M)| \le \log \bar{m}$, hence
$|\log(\mu_s/M)| \le (\log \bar{m})/\hat\kappa$, and the bound follows.
(iv) $\mathcal{R}$ is a function of $\mu$ and carries no information about any
outcome, so restricting both the calibration and the test cells to $\mathcal{R}$
gives coverage conditional on the selection event.
\end{IEEEproof}

One dependence deserves stating, because it is the place a careful reader will
push. $M$ is the mean of the same $\mu$ vector being deflated, so
$\hat{\lambda}_s$ is not a function of cell $s$ alone: every cell enters through
$M$. Two consequences. The marginal statement (ii) should be read conditional on
$M$, which costs nothing asymptotically --- $M$ concentrates at rate
$S^{-1/2}$, and $S = 4000$ in our simulation --- but is not exactly
finite-sample. And the selection rule in (iv) is likewise not a per-cell function
of covariates, which is what a textbook split-conformal argument would want.
Exchangeability survives regardless: $M$ is a symmetric function of the cells, so
permuting cells permutes $(\hat{\lambda}_s)$ and the retention indicators
together, leaving the joint law invariant. That is all conformal validity
requires. Estimating $M$ on the calibration split alone would remove the
dependence entirely at the cost of a noisier normalizer, and we flag it as the
cleaner choice for a deployment where exact finite-sample validity matters more
than efficiency.

Part (iv) is the honest content of the empirical result in
Section~\ref{sec:feedback}: coverage is restored \emph{on the cells the system is
willing to speak about}. We set $\kappa_{\mathrm{run}} = 0.9$ and $\bar{m} = 5$
following the implementation, and we report the retained fraction wherever
corrected coverage appears.

A caveat on identification, which we would rather state than let a reader assume
away. The difference-in-differences design identifies the recording elasticity
$\rho$; the loop gain is $\kappa = \beta\rho$, and the DiD carries an uncancelled
term in the unobserved latent level, so a separately assumed policy elasticity
$\beta$ is required. $\kappa$ is therefore \emph{not} point-identified by this
design alone, and on our real municipal data the DiD is a null. We validate the
correction where the truth is available --- in simulation --- and treat real-data
results as a sensitivity analysis at an assumed gain.

\subsection{When the recording model is wrong}
\label{sec:sensitivity}
Theorem~\ref{thm:deflation}(i) is exact, but it is exact \emph{given} the
power-law fixed point. The sharpest objection to the whole construction is
therefore that the true recording mechanism may not be that power law, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:deflation}(iii) bounds only the error from a wrong $\kappa$, not
from a wrong functional form. We answer this with a marginal sensitivity model in
the manner of Rosenbaum. Suppose the true multiplier lies within a factor
$\Gamma \ge 1$ of the assumed one for every cell,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:gamma_band}
m^{\mathrm{true}}_s / m_s \in [\Gamma^{-1},\, \Gamma]
\quad\text{for all } s,
\end{equation}
which implies $\lambda_s / \hat{\lambda}_s \in [\Gamma^{-1}, \Gamma]$ directly. A
$\Gamma$-inflated interval, taking its lower endpoint at $\hat{\lambda}_s/\Gamma$
and its upper at $\hat{\lambda}_s\Gamma$, then covers a
$\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_s)$ draw for \emph{every} recording model admitted by
\eqref{eq:gamma_band}, and $\Gamma = 1$ recovers the plain corrected interval.

The point of stating it this way is that it is measurable. Building worlds whose
true multiplier deviates from the assumed one by a bounded per-cell factor, at
$\kappa = 0.6$ and target $0.90$, the plain corrected interval loses latent
coverage as the deviation grows --- $0.942$, $0.922$, $0.878$, $0.810$, $0.679$
across deviation factors $1.0$ to $3.0$, dropping below target once the factor
reaches $1.6$ --- while the $\Gamma$-inflated interval holds $0.942$ to $0.998$
throughout, at a width cost rising smoothly from $1.00\times$ to $3.05\times$.
So the assumption is not load-bearing in the sense of being unfalsifiable: it
converts into a stated envelope, and the price of widening that envelope is
known. What the plain interval cannot do is survive misspecification silently,
which is the failure mode this paper exists to remove.

% =====================================================================
\section{Method}
% =====================================================================
\subsection{Problem setup and ZINB likelihood}
Let $s \in \{1,\dots,S\}$ index spatial units, $t \in \{1,\dots,T\}$ weeks, and
$c \in \{1,\dots,C\}$ crime categories (violent, property, drug, so $C = 3$).
Chicago has $S = 77$ community areas, New York $S = 78$ comparable units, and
both panels run $T = 313$ weeks. For every triple we predict a distribution over
counts rather than a number.

Crime counts are sparse and overdispersed at once, and the two need separate
machinery: sparsity is structural, since a cell can be zero because nothing
happened or because nothing was recorded, so a point mass at zero describes the
data rather than merely simplifying it. The model emits $(\pi,\mu,r)$ per cell
as in \eqref{eq:zinb},
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:zinb}
P(Y = y) =
\begin{cases}
\pi + (1-\pi)\, f_{\mathrm{NB}}(0), & y = 0,\\[2pt]
(1-\pi)\, f_{\mathrm{NB}}(y),       & y > 0,
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
where the negative binomial mass is
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:nb}
f_{\mathrm{NB}}(y) = \frac{\Gamma(y+r)}{\Gamma(r)\,y!}
  \left(\frac{r}{r+\mu}\right)^{\!r}
  \left(\frac{\mu}{r+\mu}\right)^{\!y}.
\end{equation}
Here $\pi \in (0,1)$ is the zero-inflation probability, the mass placed on a
structural zero; $\mu > 0$ is the mean of the negative binomial component; and
$r > 0$ is its dispersion parameter, with variance $\mu + \mu^2/r$, so small $r$
means heavy-tailed and $r \to \infty$ recovers a Poisson. The network produces
them as $\pi = \sigma(\cdot)$, $\mu = \mathrm{softplus}(\cdot)$ and
$r = \mathrm{softplus}(\cdot) + 0.1$. That floor on $r$ matters more than it
looks; see Section~\ref{sec:rcollapse}.

We reuse $\pi$ for the zero-inflation probability only. The allocation policy of
Section~\ref{sec:theory} is written $\varphi$ throughout to keep the two apart.

\subsection{Architecture}
Space first. Two adjacency structures feed a GATv2 encoder: queen contiguity for
immediate geographic spillover, and $k$-nearest neighbours in demographic feature
space for areas that behave alike without touching. Attention is computed
dynamically over the union of both neighbourhoods,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:gat}
\begin{aligned}
e_{ij} &= \mathbf{z}^{\!\top} \mathrm{LeakyReLU}
          \!\left(\mathbf{W}[\mathbf{h}_i \,\|\, \mathbf{h}_j]\right),\\
\gamma_{ij} &= \frac{\exp(e_{ij})}{\sum_{k \in \mathcal{N}_i}\exp(e_{ik})},
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
with $\mathcal{N}_i = \mathcal{N}^{\mathrm{queen}}_i \cup
\mathcal{N}^{\mathrm{knn}}_i$ in \eqref{eq:gat}, and node states update as the
attention-weighted sum over that union.

Then time. A causal Transformer consumes the GATv2 node states in sequence, so
space and time are encoded in stages rather than jointly. We implemented a
unified variant that attends over space--time tokens with a structured mask as
well, but every number in this paper comes from the staged configuration, and we
describe the system we actually evaluated.

Between the two sits a multi-factor feature mixer: soft-attention heads over the
fused embedding, regularized by a Jensen--Shannon penalty between head pairs. We
want to be exact about what that penalty does, because it is easy to overstate. It
prevents \emph{head collapse} --- it fires when two heads' attention
distributions grow too similar, keeping the factor decomposition non-degenerate.
It is not a fairness mechanism and it does not decorrelate representations from
protected attributes. The architecture does contain a gradient-reversal
adversarial discriminator for demographic invariance in the manner of Ganin
\emph{et al.}, but it is disabled in the configuration reported here, so the
trained predictor carries \emph{no} representation-level guard against proxy
discrimination. What fairness we can demonstrate is downstream and post hoc: the
coverage-disparity ceiling of Section~\ref{sec:calibration}, audited in
Section~\ref{sec:conformal}. Section~\ref{sec:limitations} states the consequence.

We anchor $\mu$ to a trailing mean rather than predicting it free. This was not a
preference: without anchoring, conformal interval widths exceed 1000 and skill
score goes deeply negative. Anchoring holds the level and lets the network model
deviations from it.

\subsection{Training and the $r$-collapse problem}
\label{sec:rcollapse}
Training minimizes ZINB negative log-likelihood, computed with
$\mathrm{logsumexp}$ on the zero branch and $\log\Gamma$ elsewhere for stability.

One failure mode deserves description, because it is a clean example of a metric
lying. Under maximum likelihood, $r$ drifts toward its floor. As $r \to 0$ the
negative binomial variance $\mu + \mu^2/r$ implied by \eqref{eq:nb} diverges,
giving a heavy-tailed
distribution that assigns tolerable probability to almost any observation, so NLL
looks acceptable. MAE even improves, because the mode sharpens. But CRPS
degrades, because the predictive CDF is smeared. Likelihood and sharpness pull in
opposite directions and likelihood wins. The fix is the per-cell penalty
\eqref{eq:rreg},
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:rreg}
\mathcal{L}_{r\text{-reg}}
 = \lambda_r \cdot \frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}|}
   \sum_{i \in \mathcal{B}} \mathrm{ReLU}(r_{\mathrm{reg}} - r_i),
\end{equation}
with $r_{\mathrm{reg}} = 0.5$ and $\lambda_r = 0.1$. Per-cell rather than
batch-mean is the whole point: a batch-mean penalty lets some cells collapse to
near zero while others compensate by staying high, so the average looks fine
while individual predictive distributions are useless.

\subsection{Calibration}
\label{sec:calibration}
The model's own quantiles are not trustworthy, so we calibrate post hoc, on a
chronological split that never lets a later period inform an earlier one. Fix a
miscoverage level $\alpha$, so the target coverage is $1-\alpha$; we use
$\alpha = 0.1$ throughout. Let $q_p(x_i)$ denote the level-$p$ quantile of the
ZINB predictive distribution for a cell with covariates $x_i$, and let $n$ be the
number of calibration cells. Non-conformity uses the CQR score
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:cqr}
V_i = \max\!\left(q_{\alpha/2}(x_i) - y_i,\; y_i - q_{1-\alpha/2}(x_i)\right),
\end{equation}
which is positive when $y_i$ falls outside the predictive interval and negative
when it falls inside, and the split-conformal threshold is the
$\lceil (n+1)(1-\alpha) \rceil / n$ empirical quantile of
$\{V_1,\dots,V_n\}$. For per-group control over $G$ demographic groups, ECRC
computes a separate threshold per group with the Hoeffding slack
\eqref{eq:ecrc},
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:ecrc}
\epsilon_g = \sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\delta_g)}{2 n_g}},
\end{equation}
where $n_g$ is the number of calibration cells in group $g$ and $\delta_g$ is
that group's failure probability, Bonferroni-corrected as $\delta_g = \delta / G$
so the guarantee holds simultaneously across groups at level $\delta$. Group
coverage is then at least $1 - \alpha - \epsilon_g$ with probability
$1-\delta_g$. An adaptive temporal variant updates the per-group miscoverage
target online with a PID rule~\cite{angelopoulos2023conformal}; it gives a
long-run average guarantee, not a per-step one, and we report it as such.

We evaluate ten variants and select among them by constraint rather than by eye:
narrowest mean width subject to marginal coverage at or above the floor,
demographic disparity at or below 0.03, abstention at or below 1\%, and finite
metrics. The ceiling was fixed before we looked. Section~\ref{sec:conformal}
shows the constraint doing real work.

Two of the ten deserve a word here, because between them they cover the
reweighting family a reader may reasonably expect to solve the problem outright.
Our weighted variant assigns exponentially decaying weights to calibration points
by recency and takes a weighted quantile of the scores, which targets
non-stationarity: recent weeks count for more when the panel drifts. Weighted CP
in the covariate-shift sense~\cite{tibshirani2019conformal} instead weights by a
covariate likelihood ratio $w(x)$. Neither addresses the problem of
Section~\ref{sec:theory}, and for the same structural reason: reweighting changes
\emph{which calibration points count}, never \emph{what the score measures}. Every
$V_i$ in \eqref{eq:cqr} is a function of the recorded $y_i$, so any weighted
quantile of $\{V_i\}$ --- uniform, recency-decayed, density-ratio, or adaptively
updated --- certifies coverage of $y$ and is silent about $\lambda$. The family is
closed under the wrong target. Leaving it requires changing the target variable,
which is what Theorem~\ref{thm:deflation} does.

Table~\ref{tab:conformal_fairness} bears this out without embarrassing the method.
Our weighted variant clears the coverage floor in both cities (0.9075 Chicago,
0.9326 NYC). On NYC it is numerically indistinguishable from split CP, where the
integer score lattice leaves the weights nothing to move; on Chicago it does shift
the interval, to 0.9075 against split CP's 0.9405. So the weights act. They act on
the right variable for drift and the wrong one for feedback.

Two smaller decisions worth recording. Ensemble weights come from
entropy-regularized EMOS~\cite{gneiting2005calibrated} learned on calibration
data, falling back to uniform when the learned weights fail to beat uniform on an
internal holdout; the entropy term exists because unregularized EMOS placed
99.6\% of its mass on a single seed. And post-hoc distributional recalibration is
\emph{fitted but gated}: we compare recalibrated against original CRPS on an
internal calibration holdout, never on test, and apply the correction only if it
helps. On both cities it did not (Chicago $-5.29\%$, NYC $-0.66\%$), so both
report identity recalibration. Gating on test CRPS would have been leakage.

\subsection{Feedback-corrected latent intervals}
\label{sec:latent}
Everything in Section~\ref{sec:calibration} delivers coverage of $y$, the record.
Under \eqref{eq:fixedpoint} that is not coverage of $\lambda$, and the gap widens
with $\kappa$. Two worlds --- one with honest recording, one with a biased loop
--- can produce identical records, so no test on passive data separates
them~\cite{mendler2022anticipating}. This is the ``confidently wrong'' state:
coverage of the record holds while coverage of the truth silently fails.

Breaking the tie needs a perturbation. A staggered detection-sensitivity shock
shifts recording intensity for treated units, and a difference-in-differences on
log recorded rates estimates the recording response, subject to the
identification caveat in Section~\ref{sec:theory}. Given a gain estimate, we
deflate by \eqref{eq:deflation} and issue intervals on $\hat\lambda$.

Abstention is not optional. By Theorem~\ref{thm:deflation}(iii) the log-error
scales with $\log(\mu_s/M)$, which is unbounded, so we abstain when $\hat\kappa$
exceeds $\kappa_{\mathrm{run}} = 0.9$ or the required multiplier leaves
$[1/5, 5]$. The system says ``I do not know'' rather than issuing an interval it
cannot stand behind. That is the right behaviour, and it has a real cost that
Section~\ref{sec:feedback} measures rather than leaves implicit.
Algorithm~\ref{alg:civic_safe} details the complete feedback-corrected
conformal inference procedure, from non-conformity thresholding on the
calibration split to query evaluation, safety-gated abstention, and latent interval
issuance.

\begin{algorithm}[!t]
\caption{Feedback-Corrected Latent Conformal Prediction (\textsf{CIVIC-SAFE})}
\label{alg:civic_safe}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\REQUIRE Test input $x_{T+1, s}$ for spatial unit $s$, trained forecaster
$f_\theta$, nominal miscoverage $\alpha \in (0,1)$, estimated feedback gain
$\hat{\kappa}$, panel scale $M = S^{-1}\sum_s \hat{\mu}_s$, multiplier bound
$\bar{m} = 5$, runaway threshold $\kappa_{\mathrm{run}} = 0.9$, sensitivity factor
$\Gamma \ge 1$ ($\Gamma = 1$ in the reported results).
\ENSURE Latent rate estimate $\hat{\lambda}_s$ and interval $\widehat{C}_s$, or
abstention token $\bot$.
\STATE Predict recorded parameters:
       $(\hat{\pi}_s, \hat{\mu}_s, \hat{r}_s) \leftarrow f_\theta(x_{T+1, s})$.
\STATE Recording multiplier: $m_s \leftarrow (\hat{\mu}_s / M)^{\hat{\kappa}}$.
\STATE \textbf{Abstention gate} (Theorem~\ref{thm:deflation}(iii)--(iv)):
\IF{$\hat{\kappa} \ge \kappa_{\mathrm{run}}$}
  \STATE \textbf{return} $\bot$ \COMMENT{global: correction variance unbounded}
\ELSIF{$m_s \notin [\bar{m}^{-1},\, \bar{m}]$}
  \STATE \textbf{return} $\bot$ \COMMENT{per-cell: deflation outside safe envelope}
\ENDIF
\STATE Deflate to the latent rate (Theorem~\ref{thm:deflation}(i)):
       $\hat{\lambda}_s \leftarrow \hat{\mu}_s / m_s
        = M^{\hat{\kappa}}\, \hat{\mu}_s^{\,1-\hat{\kappa}}$.
\STATE \textbf{Latent interval} (Theorem~\ref{thm:deflation}(ii)); the $\Gamma$
       band is \eqref{eq:gamma_band}:
       \[
       \widehat{C}_s \leftarrow \left[\,
         Q^{\mathrm{Pois}}_{\alpha/2}\!\left(\hat{\lambda}_s/\Gamma\right),\;
         Q^{\mathrm{Pois}}_{1-\alpha/2}\!\left(\hat{\lambda}_s\Gamma\right)
       \,\right].
       \]
\STATE \textbf{return} $\hat{\lambda}_s,\; \widehat{C}_s$.
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

Two features of Algorithm~\ref{alg:civic_safe} are worth flagging because they are
easy to get wrong. It carries \emph{no} additive conformity margin: by
Theorem~\ref{thm:deflation}(ii) the Poisson quantiles at the deflated rate are
already conservative when $\hat\kappa = \kappa$, and the honest response to
$\hat\kappa \ne \kappa$ is the multiplicative $\Gamma$ band of
Section~\ref{sec:sensitivity}, not an additive widening calibrated on the
record --- a record-calibrated margin would import exactly the bias the deflation
removes. Our implementation exposes an additive margin as an option; it is zero in
every number reported here. And the two abstention branches are distinct
mechanisms with distinct causes, which Section~\ref{sec:feedback} separates
empirically: the global branch responds to the estimated gain, the per-cell branch
to the required deflation.

% =====================================================================
\section{Experimental Setup}
% =====================================================================
\textbf{Data.} Chicago (77 community areas) and New York (78 units), weekly
counts in three categories over 2018--2023, giving $T = 313$ weeks. The split is
strictly chronological, by week index: train $[0, 208)$ = 2018--2021, validation
$[208, 234)$ = 2022 H1 (early stopping and per-seed EMA-versus-raw selection),
calibration $[234, 260)$ = 2022 H2 (conformal thresholds and EMOS weights), test
$[260, 313)$ = 2023, the 53 weeks on which every number in this paper is
computed. Nothing from a later block informs an earlier one. Chicago test tensors
are $53 \times 77$. Demographic groups for the fairness audit come from
area-level composition and are fixed before evaluation.

\textbf{Baselines.} Six classical model families --- historical average, seasonal
naive, lag-1 persistence, STARIMA, plain ZINB and XGBoost --- with the historical
average evaluated in both a rolling and a frozen variant. Four deep
spatiotemporal models: LSTM-NB, TFT-ZINB, GraphWaveNet, STZINB-GNN. Deep
baselines run three seeds ($42, 137, 256$), reported as mean $\pm$ standard
deviation.

\textbf{Metrics.} CRPS is primary, being a strictly proper scoring rule for
distributional forecasts. We also report MAE, RMSE and Brier score on the zero
event. For calibration: marginal coverage, mean width, per-group and per-category
disparity, abstention rate, PIT uniformity $\chi^2$, and the Hersbach
decomposition~\cite{hersbach2000decomposition} of CRPS into reliability,
resolution and uncertainty.

\textbf{Significance.} Diebold--Mariano~\cite{diebold1995comparing} with
Newey--West adjustment on paired weekly losses, plus a stationary block
bootstrap. We treat a claim as supported only when both agree.

\textbf{Which baseline binds.} CRPSS against a \emph{frozen} historical average
looks impressive --- 0.2713 and 0.3165. We do not lead with it. A frozen baseline
is unrealistically weak, because a real deployment would update its average as
weeks arrive. Against a \emph{rolling} HA the gains are 0.0360 and 0.0494, and
the evaluation code marks \texttt{ha\_rolling} as binding. Those are the numbers
we quote.

\section{Results}
% =====================================================================
\input{tables/table1_main_results}

\subsection{Predictive accuracy}
Table~\ref{tab:main_results} reports the main benchmark. CRPS 2.8267 and 3.1401,
best in both cities; MAE 3.9017 and 4.3675; RMSE 7.0983 and 7.6126; Brier on the
zero event 0.0592 and 0.0493.

Fig.~\ref{fig:coverage_convergence} shows empirical coverage converging to the
nominal level from above as the calibration set grows, which is what the integer
score lattice of \eqref{eq:cqr} predicts.

The Diebold--Mariano results are clean. Against all four deep baselines in both
cities --- eight comparisons --- CIVIC-SAFE wins every one at $p < 2\times10^{-6}$:
GraphWaveNet ($-9.319$, $-15.321$), LSTM-NB ($-7.482$ at
$7.33\!\times\!10^{-14}$, $-6.979$ at $2.97\!\times\!10^{-12}$), STZINB-GNN
($-10.186$, $-11.158$) and TFT-ZINB ($-4.790$ at $1.67\!\times\!10^{-6}$,
$-7.669$ at $1.73\!\times\!10^{-14}$). Against the rolling HA the margin is real
but much smaller: Chicago DM $p = 0.0338$ with bootstrap $p = 0.0053$, NYC
$p = 0.0036$ with bootstrap $p = 0.0003$. Both tests agree in both cities, which
is what we required. Fig.~\ref{fig:crpss} plots the skill scores.

\begin{figure}[!t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig1_coverage_convergence.pdf}
  \caption{Empirical coverage against calibration-set size. The horizontal axis
  is the number of calibration points $n$; the vertical axis is realized marginal
  coverage on held-out data, with the dashed line at the nominal
  $1-\alpha = 0.90$. Coverage approaches the target from above, consistent with
  split conformal's finite-sample band $[1-\alpha,\, 1-\alpha + 1/(n+1)]$; the
  residual excess persisting at large $n$ is the lattice effect, since integer CQR
  scores cannot realize an arbitrary quantile level exactly.}
  \label{fig:coverage_convergence}
\end{figure}

Ensembling is doing heavy lifting, and it would be dishonest to imply otherwise.
A single model averages CRPS 3.3622, worse than TFT-ZINB's 2.9456 on Chicago.
Five-seed EMOS takes it to 2.8267, a 16\% improvement. The architecture alone
does not win. Table~\ref{tab:ensemble} gives the ensemble-size sweep,
Table~\ref{tab:ablation} the component ablation, and
Table~\ref{tab:loss_ablation} the loss-function ablation.

There is a harder fact in Table~\ref{tab:main_results} that we want to put in
front of the reader rather than leave to be discovered. The rolling historical
average beats \emph{every} deep spatiotemporal baseline we ran, in both cities:
2.9322 against LSTM-NB's 3.1037, TFT-ZINB's 2.9456, GraphWaveNet's 3.1189 and
STZINB-GNN's 3.3222 on Chicago, and 3.3034 against 3.3426, 3.4244, 3.8857 and
3.6921 on NYC. Eight comparisons, eight wins for the trailing mean. So the
eight-of-eight Diebold--Mariano result above, impressive as the $p$-values look,
establishes that we beat a set of models that a four-week moving average also
beats. The claim worth making is the narrower one: of everything in this study,
CIVIC-SAFE is the only method that improves on the trailing mean, and it does so
by 3.6\% and 4.9\%. Weekly area-level crime counts are strongly mean-reverting,
and any paper in this area that does not report a rolling-average baseline should
be read with that in mind.

\input{tables/table4_ablation}
\input{tables/table5_loss_ablation}
\input{tables/table6_ensemble}

\input{tables/table3_uncertainty}

The Hersbach decomposition (Table~\ref{tab:uncertainty}, Fig.~\ref{fig:hersbach})
locates the remaining error, but it needs reading carefully and we would rather
set out the caveat than let the numbers flatter us. Resolution and climatological
uncertainty are on the count scale, in CRPS units. The reliability term as we
compute it is a Cram\'er--von Mises-type statistic on the cumulative PIT, so it
is a squared probability and \emph{not} commensurable with the other two; the
ratio $\mathrm{REL}/\mathrm{RES}$ is therefore not a fraction of forecast loss
and we do not report it as one. Our resolution is also obtained by residual from
the identity $\mathrm{CRPS} = \mathrm{REL} - \mathrm{RES} + \mathrm{UNC}$, which
makes the decomposition an accounting identity rather than an independent check:
the reconstructed CRPS agrees with the measured CRPS by construction and cannot
fail to.

What the term does carry is a comparison. Chicago's reliability is $0.00124$
against NYC's $0.00006$, a factor of $20.6$, and Chicago's cumulative PIT
deviation reaches $4.95$ percentage points with every bin deviating in the same
direction. That is a systematic miscalibration, not noise, and it agrees with the
independent $\chi^2$ PIT test (ratio $22.5$, Section~\ref{sec:limitations}). So
the honest reading is the relative one: Chicago is roughly twenty times worse
calibrated than NYC, and the CRPSS against climatology ($0.7693$, $0.7732$) is
the well-posed absolute statement --- both cities extract about $77\%$ of the
available skill over a climatological forecast.

\begin{figure}[!t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig4_crps_decomposition.pdf}
  \caption{Hersbach decomposition of CRPS for both cities. Bars give reliability
  (REL), resolution (RES) and climatological uncertainty (UNC); lower REL and
  higher RES are better. RES and UNC are on the count scale; REL is a squared
  cumulative-PIT statistic and so is not commensurable with them, which is why we
  compare REL only across cities (Chicago $20.6\times$ NYC) and not as a share of
  CRPS. RES is obtained by residual from
  $\mathrm{CRPS} = \mathrm{REL} - \mathrm{RES} + \mathrm{UNC}$.}
  \label{fig:hersbach}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Where the errors live in space}
\label{sec:spatial}
Averaging the residual (predicted minus actual violent count) over the 53 test
weeks for each of Chicago's 77 community areas turns up something the aggregate
metrics hide. \textbf{65 of 77 areas are under-predicted.} The mean residual is
$-1.03$ incidents per area--week, the median $-0.52$, and the range is lopsided:
$-8.31$ at worst against only $+1.40$ at the other end. Predicted counts top out
at 102 where actual counts reach 133.

The bias is not spread evenly. Correlating each area's mean residual against its
mean actual count gives $-0.66$ --- the busiest areas are under-predicted most.
Fig.~\ref{fig:spatial_error} maps it, and the shortfall concentrates visibly on
Chicago's West Side, which is where violent crime is highest.

We point this out because it independently confirms what the PIT test says in
Section~\ref{sec:limitations}. Two diagnostics computed in completely different
ways --- a distributional uniformity test on the probability integral transform,
and a plain spatial average of signed errors --- agree that the model compresses
Chicago's upper tail. That is more convincing than either alone, and it locates
the problem: not diffuse noise, but a systematic shortfall in the highest-count
areas.

\begin{figure}[!t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.86\linewidth]{spatial_error_map.png}
  \caption{Mean signed residual per Chicago community area, violent crime, over
  the 53-week 2023 test set. Each area is shaded by
  $\overline{\hat{y} - y}$, the time-averaged prediction minus observation, on a
  diverging scale centred at zero: blue is under-prediction, red over-prediction,
  white unbiased. $65$ of $77$ areas are negative, the mean residual is $-1.03$
  incidents per area-week, and the correlation between an area's mean count and its
  residual is $-0.66$, so the shortfall concentrates in the busiest areas. The
  clustering on the West Side is spatial structure, not diffuse noise, and it
  corroborates the PIT failure in Fig.~
ef{fig:pit} by an independent route.}
  \label{fig:spatial_error}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Conformal calibration and the constraint that bites}
\label{sec:conformal}
Nine variants, target 90\%, disparity ceiling 0.03 fixed in advance.
Table~\ref{tab:conformal_fairness} reports coverage, width, demographic and
category disparity, and abstention for both cities;
Fig.~\ref{fig:conformal_comparison} shows the coverage--width trade-off.

\input{tables/table2_conformal_fairness}

Selected coverage is 90.75\% (Chicago, equalized coverage) and 90.02\% (NYC,
variance-scaled split CP) against a 90\% target, with disparity 0.0238 and
0.0286 and abstention zero everywhere. NYC clears the ceiling by 0.0014 --- one
resampling from failing --- and we are not going to describe that as
comfortable.

\begin{figure}[!t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig5_conformal_comparison.pdf}
  \caption{Coverage against mean interval width for the ten conformal variants.
  Each marker is one calibration method; the horizontal axis is mean interval
  width in counts (lower is better) and the vertical axis is marginal coverage on
  the 2023 test set. The dashed horizontal line is the pre-registered $90\%$
  coverage floor. Methods below that line are rejected by policy however narrow
  they are, which is what excludes rolling adaptive ECRC despite its being the
  narrowest and least disparate variant in both cities.}
  \label{fig:conformal_comparison}
\end{figure}

Three observations. First, the constraint is load-bearing. Rolling adaptive ECRC
has the best disparity in both cities (0.0013, 0.0046) and the narrowest
intervals (13.88, 16.31), and a width-minimizing selection would have taken it.
Its coverage is 89.30\% and 89.18\%, below the floor, so the policy rejected it.
A fairness constraint that never rejects anything is decoration; this one changed
the answer.

Second, four NYC methods are numerically identical --- split CP, weighted CP,
Mondrian and equalized coverage all report $0.9326 / 18.57 / 0.0201$. That is the
signature of a degenerate conformity threshold: CQR scores on this panel are
integers, so methods differing only in \emph{how} they select a quantile collapse
onto the same lattice point. It tells you something about the data rather than
the code.

Third, per-category coverage spreads wider than the marginal number suggests.
Chicago: violent 0.8883, property 0.8829, drug 0.9515 --- two of three categories
below 90\%, a spread of 0.069. NYC: violent 0.8677, property 0.8950, drug 0.9378.
Marginal coverage can look fine while specific categories are undercovered.
Fig.~\ref{fig:pit} contrasts the two cities' PIT histograms, which is the
distributional version of the same story.

\begin{figure}[!t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig2_pit_histogram.pdf}
  \caption{PIT histograms for both cities. The horizontal axis is the randomized
  probability integral transform value on $[0,1]$, binned into ten equal
  intervals; the vertical axis is the relative frequency of test cells falling in
  each bin. A correctly specified predictive distribution gives a flat histogram
  at $0.10$ per bin, marked by the dashed line. NYC is indistinguishable from
  uniform ($\chi^2 = 10.75$ on nine degrees of freedom, $p = 0.293$). Chicago is
  not ($\chi^2 = 241.84$, $p = 5.25\times10^{-47}$): mass rises monotonically
  across the upper bins, reaching $13.68\%$ in the top bin against the expected
  $10\%$. Excess mass at high PIT values means observations land further into the
  right tail than the model expects, i.e. a compressed upper tail.}
  \label{fig:pit}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Decision-theoretic allocation}
We simulate patrol allocation across four policies at three budgets
(Table~\ref{tab:policy-simulation}, Fig.~\ref{fig:policy}). At $B = 100$, OICC
captures the most violent incidents in both cities, 96.36\% and 98.97\%, and
reduces the demographic over-allocation ratio substantially --- Chicago from
1.036 to 0.643, NYC from 1.030 to 0.865 --- meaning it stops over-policing groups
relative to their incident share.

\input{tables/table7_policy_simulation}

But the allocation-disparity column is the worst of the four policies in both
cities: 0.1448 against 0.0132 for unconstrained conformal on Chicago, eleven
times larger. These two fairness metrics genuinely disagree. Over-allocation
ratio measures policing relative to where incidents are; allocation disparity
measures evenness across groups. OICC improves the first by concentrating
resources differently, and that concentration is exactly what worsens the second.
We report both, because reporting only the favourable one would be selective, and
a reader deciding whether to deploy this needs to know which notion of fairness
they are buying. At $B = 20$ OICC is also worst on hit rate --- 0.5242 against
0.5677 on Chicago, 0.4896 against 0.5014 on NYC. The advantage appears only at
larger budgets.

\begin{figure*}[!t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.92\textwidth]{fig9_policy_tradeoff.pdf}
  \caption{Violent-incident hit rate against allocation disparity for four
  patrol-allocation policies at budgets $B \in \{20, 50, 100\}$, both cities. The
  horizontal axis is allocation disparity across demographic groups (lower is more
  even); the vertical axis is the fraction of violent incidents falling inside
  allocated units (higher is better). Up-and-left is better on both criteria at
  once. OICC attains the best hit rate at $B = 100$ in both cities
  ($96.36\%$, $98.97\%$) and simultaneously the \emph{worst} allocation disparity
  ($0.1448$, $0.0421$), so no policy dominates: the two fairness criteria move in
  opposite directions, and OICC's gain on over-allocation ratio is bought with
  concentration that allocation disparity penalizes.}
  \label{fig:policy}
\end{figure*}

\subsection{The feedback correction}
\label{sec:feedback}
This is the result the paper is for. We simulate a closed loop at known feedback
gain, so the latent rate is available for scoring --- the only setting in which
coverage of the truth can be measured at all.

\begin{table}[!t]
  \centering
  \caption{Coverage of the latent process under observation-biased feedback
  (simulation, $4000$ cells, $12$ trials, target $1-\alpha = 0.90$). Naive
  coverage is measured on all cells; corrected coverage only on retained cells.
  The final column is why those two numbers are not directly comparable.}
  \label{tab:feedback}
  \footnotesize
  \begin{tabular}{c r r r r}
    \toprule
    $\kappa$ & \textbf{Naive} & $\hat\kappa$ \textbf{(DiD)} &
      \textbf{Corrected} & \textbf{Retained} \\
    \midrule
    0.00 & 0.950 & 0.259 & 0.949 & 75\% \\
    0.30 & 0.903 & 0.300 & 0.952 & 100\% \\
    0.50 & 0.780 & 0.500 & 0.948 & 95\% \\
    0.70 & 0.502 & 0.713 & 0.937 & 56\% \\
    0.85 & \textbf{0.162} & 0.850 & \textbf{0.930} & \textbf{15\%} \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

Read the naive column of Table~\ref{tab:feedback} first. Intervals calibrated on the record, targeting 90\%,
cover the latent process 95.0\% of the time at $\kappa = 0$ and 16.2\% at
$\kappa = 0.85$. The intervals never stopped being valid for the record. They
simply stopped being about reality, and nothing in a standard validation pipeline
would show it.

The corrected column holds 93.0\% at $\kappa = 0.85$. The DiD recovers the gain
well in the middle of the range ($0.300, 0.500, 0.713, 0.850$ against true
$0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.85$) and poorly at zero, where $\hat\kappa = 0.259$ against a
true $0$. That upward bias at zero gain is a real limitation of the estimator and
we report it rather than trimming the row.

Now the cost, which we want stated as plainly as the benefit. The last column is
the fraction of cells the corrector keeps. At $\kappa = 0.85$ it abstains on 85\%
of them, so 93.0\% is measured on the surviving 15\% while the naive 16.2\% is
measured on all cells. \textbf{The two columns have different denominators.} This
is exactly what Theorem~\ref{thm:deflation}(iv) formalizes: the guarantee is
conditional on retention. The comparison still means something --- on the cells
where correction is trustworthy, coverage of the truth is restored from
catastrophic to near-nominal --- but anyone who reads $16\% \to 93\%$ as
like-for-like has been misled, so Fig.~\ref{fig:latent} carries the retained
fraction as a second panel and we label it wherever it appears.

Two properties of the $\kappa = 0$ row deserve to be read deliberately, because
between them they answer the question a sceptical reader should ask first: does the
correction manufacture the effect it reports? At zero gain there is nothing to
correct, and the correction does nothing. Latent coverage moves from $0.950$ to
$0.949$, and in the routing experiment of Fig.~\ref{fig:routing} disparity moves
from $0.287$ to $0.287$ with a reduction of exactly $0.000$. The procedure is
\emph{inert on an unbiased record}. That is a negative control, and it is the
reason the reductions at higher gain can be attributed to the loop rather than to
the machinery: a method that shrank disparity at $\kappa = 0$ would be shrinking it
for some reason other than feedback.

The same row also costs something, and the mechanism is not the one we first
assumed. At $\kappa = 0$ the corrector abstains on a quarter of cells while
improving nothing. The natural reading is that the per-cell multiplier bound
$\bar{m}$ is mistuned for low gain, and that reading is wrong: at
$\hat\kappa \to 0$ the multiplier $m_s = (\hat\mu_s/M)^{\hat\kappa} \to 1$ for
every cell, so the per-cell branch cannot fire. Instrumenting the two branches
separately over $24$ trials confirms it. At $\kappa = 0$ the per-cell branch fires
on $0.0000\%$ of cells and the entire loss comes from the \emph{global} branch,
which trips whenever the difference-in-differences estimate happens to exceed
$\kappa_{\mathrm{run}}$; the estimator has median $\hat\kappa = 0.020$ but a
maximum of $0.950$, and it crossed the threshold in $12\%$ of trials. At
$\kappa = 0.85$ the picture inverts: the per-cell branch fires on $85.06\%$ of
cells and the global branch on only $4\%$ of trials. So the high-gain cost is the
deflation genuinely leaving the safe envelope, while the low-gain cost is variance
in $\hat\kappa$ tripping a tripwire that has no confidence statement attached to
it. The two need different remedies --- a tighter envelope for the first, an
interval estimate for $\hat\kappa$ rather than a point estimate for the second ---
and we have implemented neither.

\begin{figure}[!t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig10_latent_correction.pdf}
  \caption{Coverage of the latent process under observation-biased feedback.
  \emph{Upper panel}: the horizontal axis is the true feedback gain $\kappa$; the
  vertical axis is the fraction of cells whose realized latent count falls inside
  the issued interval. The red circles are intervals calibrated on the record
  (naive) and the blue squares are feedback-corrected intervals; the dashed line
  is the $90\%$ target. Naive coverage collapses from $95.0\%$ to $16.2\%$ as the
  gain rises, while corrected coverage holds between $93.0\%$ and $95.2\%$.
  \emph{Lower panel}: the fraction of cells retained, that is, not abstained on.
  This panel is essential to reading the upper one --- corrected coverage is
  computed only over retained cells, whereas naive coverage is computed over all
  cells, so at $\kappa = 0.85$ the $93.0\%$ is measured on the $15\%$ of cells the
  corrector was willing to speak about. The two curves do not share a
  denominator, and Theorem~\ref{thm:deflation}(iv) is why.}
  \label{fig:latent}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Routing.} The same correction applied to advisory routing, with a group-1
structural over-recording factor of 1.8, cuts worst-group exposure disparity from
0.182 to 0.044 at $\kappa = 0.85$ --- a 75.8\% reduction, so routes stop
systematically steering around over-recorded areas
(Fig.~\ref{fig:routing}). The biased curve is not monotone: it falls from 0.270
to 0.182 between $\kappa = 0.70$ and $0.85$, so the worst biased case is not the
highest gain, and we do not describe the trend as monotone.

There is a check on Theorem~\ref{thm:amplification} hiding in this experiment,
and it passes. The theorem says amplification grows with the gain, so the
\emph{fraction} of disparity attributable to feedback --- and therefore the
fraction a correct deflation should remove --- ought to increase in $\kappa$ even
where the raw disparity does not. The relative reductions are $0\%$, $29.3\%$,
$47.1\%$, $67.1\%$ and $75.6\%$ across the grid: monotone in $\kappa$, including
across the $0.70 \to 0.85$ step where the absolute disparity falls. The
non-monotone absolute curve and the monotone relative curve are both what
\eqref{eq:powerlaw} predicts, which is a modest but genuine piece of evidence
that the amplification law describes the simulated mechanism rather than merely
labelling it.

\begin{figure}[!t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig11_routing_disparity.pdf}
  \caption{Worst-group exposure disparity under advisory routing. The horizontal
  axis is the feedback gain $\kappa$; the vertical axis is realized exposure
  disparity for the worst-off group, where $0$ denotes parity. Red circles route on
  the raw recorded field, blue squares on the feedback-corrected field, and the
  shaded band between them is the disparity attributable to routing on biased
  records. Group-1 structural over-recording factor is $1.8$. The biased curve is
  \emph{not} monotone (it falls from $0.270$ to $0.182$ over the last step), but
  the relative reduction is: $0\%$, $29.3\%$, $47.1\%$, $67.1\%$, $75.6\%$, as
  Theorem~
ef{thm:amplification} predicts.}
  \label{fig:routing}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Real records.} Applying the correction to actual Chicago and NYC records
at an assumed $\kappa = 0.6$ reduces exposure disparity for the higher-minority
stratum from 0.390 to 0.163 in Chicago ($-58.2\%$) and from 0.311 to 0.122 in NYC
($-60.8\%$); see Fig.~\ref{fig:crosscity}. Corollary~\ref{cor:attribution} is what
licenses reading those reductions as attribution rather than as smoothing: at
$\kappa = 0.6$ the exponent $1-\kappa = 0.4$ says that $60\%$ of any recorded
log-disparity is loop and $40\%$ is incidence, and the observed reductions of
$58\%$ and $61\%$ sit close to that predicted share. We resist making more of the
agreement than it can bear --- exposure disparity relative to population share is
not the between-group ratio $\Delta_y$ that \eqref{eq:attribution} is stated for,
so this is a consistency check on the magnitude, not a test of the corollary. Two
caveats travel with the result and must not be dropped. The gain is
\emph{assumed}, not identified --- the real-data DiD is a null --- so this is a
sensitivity analysis rather than a validated identification. And latent coverage
cannot be evaluated here at all, because the true rate is unobservable on real
data. The coverage guarantee lives in the simulation above; this shows only that
correction moves real-world allocation in the predicted direction, by roughly the
predicted amount, under a plausible gain.

\begin{figure}[!t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig12_cross_city_disparity.pdf}
  \caption{Exposure disparity for the higher-minority stratum on real municipal
  records. Bars give disparity relative to population share, red for allocation on
  the raw recorded rate and blue after feedback correction; $0$ denotes parity, and
  the annotation is the relative reduction. Chicago ($77$ community areas) falls
  from $0.390$ to $0.163$ and NYC ($78$ units) from $0.311$ to $0.122$. The gain is
  \emph{assumed} at $\kappa = 0.6$ rather than identified --- the real-data
  difference-in-differences is a null --- so this is a sensitivity analysis. Latent
  coverage cannot be evaluated here at all, because the true rate is unobservable
  on real records; Fig.~
ef{fig:latent} carries the coverage guarantee.}
  \label{fig:crosscity}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[!t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig3_crpss_comparison.pdf}
  \caption{CRPS skill score by city and crime category. Bars give
  $\mathrm{CRPSS} = 1 - \mathrm{CRPS}_{\mathrm{model}} /
  \mathrm{CRPS}_{\mathrm{baseline}}$ against the \emph{rolling} historical
  average, which the evaluation code marks as the binding baseline; positive is
  better and $0$ means parity with the baseline. Skill against a frozen historical
  average would be far larger ($0.2713$, $0.3165$) but is not the honest
  comparison, since a deployed baseline would update as weeks arrive.}
  \label{fig:crpss}
\end{figure}

% =====================================================================
\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}
% =====================================================================
We would rather list these ourselves.

\textbf{Chicago is misspecified.} The PIT histogram fails uniformity badly:
$\chi^2 = 241.84$, $p = 5.25\times10^{-47}$, maximum bin deviation 0.0368 against
an expected 0.10 per bin. The top bin holds 13.68\% of the mass and the rise
across upper bins is monotone, so the model systematically under-predicts
Chicago's right tail. NYC passes cleanly ($\chi^2 = 10.75$, $p = 0.293$), which
makes the Chicago failure a property of that city's data rather than a bug in
shared code. The spatial residuals say the same thing from another direction
(Section~\ref{sec:spatial}). Conformal coverage still holds at 90.75\%, because
split conformal's guarantee is marginal and finite-sample under exchangeability
and does not require a correctly specified model --- that is precisely why we
calibrate post hoc. But a correctly specified model would give tighter intervals,
and ours is not one.

\textbf{The correction's abstention cost is severe at high gain.} 85\% of cells
at $\kappa = 0.85$. A deployment there would decline to answer for most of the
city. That is honest behaviour and it is also a limited product.

\textbf{$\kappa$ is not point-identified.} The DiD gives the recording elasticity
$\rho$; the loop gain $\kappa = \beta\rho$ needs an assumed policy elasticity
$\beta$, and the DiD carries an uncancelled latent-level term. Real-data results
are sensitivity analyses at assumed $\kappa$. On real data our DiD is a null.
Section~\ref{sec:sensitivity} converts the functional-form assumption into a
measurable $\Gamma$-envelope, but the gain itself remains assumed.

\textbf{The architecture does not win on its own.} Single-seed CRPS around 3.3622
loses to TFT-ZINB's 2.9456 on Chicago. Five-seed EMOS is doing the work.

\textbf{OICC trades one fairness metric for another.} Best hit rate and best
over-allocation ratio, worst allocation disparity; at small budgets it is worst
on hit rate as well.

\textbf{Skill over a realistic baseline is modest.} 3.6\% and 4.9\% CRPSS against
the rolling HA. The 27--32\% figures are against a frozen baseline that no
deployment would use.

\textbf{Fairness here is coverage-based, and only post hoc.} Equal coverage
across groups is one notion among many, computed on area-level demographic
composition rather than individual attributes, and it says nothing about whether
the underlying allocation is just. It is also the \emph{only} fairness mechanism
active in the reported configuration: the gradient-reversal adversarial
discriminator that would enforce demographic invariance at the representation
level is implemented but switched off, so nothing prevents the encoder from
routing predictions through demographic proxies. The Jensen--Shannon penalty in
the feature mixer does not serve this purpose --- it prevents attention-head
collapse. Enabling the adversarial head and measuring whether representation-level
invariance buys anything beyond the coverage constraint is the obvious next
experiment, and we have not run it.

\textbf{The simulation is a simulation.} The coverage-restoration result assumes
our own generative model of the feedback loop. It is the only setting where latent
coverage is measurable, which is the point, but it is not field evidence.

\textbf{Five seeds is fewer than we would like.} Our configuration notes that
seven to eight seeds would be needed for paired $t$-tests at power 0.80 with
$d = 0.8$.

% =====================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
% =====================================================================
Records are not reality, and a forecaster validated only against records cannot
tell the difference. We built a spatiotemporal ZINB forecaster that is competitive
on conventional terms --- CRPS 2.8267 and 3.1401, eight of eight
Diebold--Mariano wins over deep baselines at $p < 2\times10^{-6}$, conformal
coverage of 90.75\% and 90.02\% under a pre-registered 3\% disparity ceiling ---
and then asked the question those terms cannot settle: is the model right about
crime, or only about crime records?

The simulation answers it sharply. At feedback gain 0.85 intervals that look well
calibrated against the record cover the latent process 16.2\% of the time.
Deflating the record by the fitted recording multiplier restores that to 93.0\%,
on the 15\% of cells where the correction is trustworthy enough to issue an
interval at all. Under bounded misspecification of the recording model a
$\Gamma$-inflated interval holds nominal coverage throughout, at a width cost that
grows smoothly and is tabulated. On real records from two cities the same
correction cuts exposure disparity for higher-minority areas by 58\% and 61\%
at an assumed gain.

The right reading of this is narrower than the numbers invite. Three conditions
carry the guarantee, and each is stated rather than assumed away: the recording
map is a power law, or else within a factor $\Gamma$ of one; validity is
conditional on retention, which at high gain means declining to answer for most
of the city; and the gain is not point-identified, so on real data we report
sensitivity rather than identification. Chicago's PIT failure is a further
reminder that the predictor underneath is misspecified on one of the two cities we
tested.

What survives those conditions is worth saying plainly. A failure that no
record-level validation can detect --- an interval that keeps its nominal coverage
of the record while losing five sixths of its coverage of reality --- is
correctable, by a map with an exact inverse, at a cost that can be measured
rather than hoped about. The natural next step is empirical, not theoretical: run
the detection-shock difference-in-differences on a real staggered rollout with
enough power to move the gain estimate off null. Until then the abstention rate,
not the coverage number, is the quantity to watch.

% =====================================================================
\section*{Reproducibility}
% =====================================================================
Every number reported here is either read from a result file under
\texttt{outputs/} or reproduced by running a script under \texttt{scripts/}. The
three feedback-correction figures are generated by
\texttt{scripts/make\_paper\_figures.py}, which calls the experiment functions
directly and writes the values it plotted to
\texttt{outputs/figure\_data/*.json}, so any figure can be checked against the
numbers behind it. Tables~\ref{tab:main_results}--\ref{tab:policy-simulation} are
generated by \texttt{scripts/ablation\_study.py} and converted to this
manuscript's floats by \texttt{scripts/build\_paper\_tables.py}; neither is
hand-edited. The spatial residual map is computed from the saved test predictions
in \texttt{outputs/conformal\_evaluation/chicago\_predictions.npz}.

Three figures that previously existed in our repository are deliberately absent.
Two attention visualizations drew synthetic weights --- an exponential distance
decay for the spatial map, a hand-built lag pattern for the temporal one --- under
titles claiming they showed learned GATv2 and transformer attention. Our pipeline
does not persist real attention weights, so those figures could not be produced
honestly, and the plotting functions now refuse to run without real input rather
than drawing something misleading.

Code and generated artifacts accompany the manuscript. The scripts named above
regenerate every table and figure from the stored evaluation outputs without
retraining, and the feedback-correction experiments are seeded, so
Table~\ref{tab:feedback} and Figs.~\ref{fig:latent}--\ref{fig:crosscity}
reproduce exactly.

% =====================================================================
\section*{Ethical Considerations}
% =====================================================================
A paper about forecasting crime should say what it is not claiming. We do not
argue that better forecasts make predictive policing appropriate, and correcting
a biased record does not make the record's provenance acceptable. What the
correction does is narrower and, we think, more useful: it makes a specific
failure \emph{visible and measurable}, namely that a model can pass every
available validation check while its intervals have stopped covering reality in
exactly the neighbourhoods that were over-policed to begin with. A system that
cannot detect that failure should not be deployed; one that can, at least
surfaces it for the people affected.

Three consequences we would want honoured by anyone building on this. The
abstention rate, not the coverage number, is the operational figure of merit: at
$\kappa = 0.85$ our corrector declines to answer for $85\%$ of cells, and a
deployment in that regime is a deployment that mostly says ``I do not know'',
which is the correct output and also a reason not to ship it. The fairness notion
we audit is equal \emph{coverage} across groups computed from area-level
composition, which is one criterion among many and says nothing about whether the
allocation it informs is just --- Section~\ref{sec:limitations} shows two
reasonable fairness metrics disagreeing about the same policy. And the routing
and allocation results are simulations of decision rules, not field trials; we
report them as evidence about the rules, not about outcomes for real people.
